newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian government expected after weekend.
newsitem.headline: New Russian government expected after weekend.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin dropped more hints on Friday on his government shake-up but, a week after liberal Anatoly Chubais was handed a leading role, the Kremlin said details would only be unveiled after the weekend.

With social discontent running deep over unpaid wages and pensions, the popular General Alexander Lebed added to pressure on Yeltsin by forecasting a descent into Albanian-style anarchy which would end with Lebed himself in the Kremlin this year.

A Kremlin spokesman said the reshuffle, ordered by Yeltsin last week to reinvigorate reforms and stave off economic crisis, would likely be announced before Yeltsin heads for Helsinki on Wednesday for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

The 66-year-old Kremlin leader, who is making his mark after a long illness, will meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday or Tuesday, the spokesman told Reuters. A decree on the reshuffle would "probably" be made public after that.
Yeltsin said on Friday the new team would be "cardinally different" from the present, though some ministers would stay.
"The most important thing is that the people who will come will have new, fresh ideas and thoughts," Interfax news agency quoted him as telling a meeting of media chiefs.

He also indicated that the upper ranks of the new cabinet may be broader than Kremlin leaks had suggested after Chubais, previously Yeltsin's chief-of-staff, was named Chernomyrdin's first deputy prime minister last Friday.

Chubais, at 41 already a veteran administrator after pushing through a dramatic privatisation programme, was said to want a tight team of allies, weeding out big industrial ministries seen as hangovers from the days of Soviet central planning.
Yeltsin, however, said the new government would include seven deputy prime ministers under Chernomyrdin and Chubais, down from nine and three first deputies in the current line-up.
That may suggest that behind-the-scenes bargaining between Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin and Chubais may have led to more of the president's older guard hanging on their jobs.
The pressure for Chubais to produce results in the face of bitter personal loathing from the communists who dominate parliament was underlined by ex-Kremlin security chief Lebed.

Russians' favourite politician in some polls and a contender to succeed Yeltsin in 2000 -- or sooner -- Lebed launched his new political movement with a warning that social tension was running so high that violence could erupt at any time.
The catalyst, the gravel-voiced paratrooper said, could be nationwide protests by trade unions planned for March 27.

"Little is needed for a few provocateurs to be introduced into any crowd during peaceful protest actions on March 27 -- broken shop windows, arson attacks, looted kiosks," said Lebed. "One victim and that's it."
Yeltsin's decision to reshuffle the cabinet and speed up reforms has prompted an angry reaction in the communist-led State Duma lower house of parliament.

In a clear attack on Yeltsin, it passed at the first reading a resolution proclaiming October 4 -- the day on which in 1993 the president crushed hardline resistance by the Soviet-era parliament -- the "Day of the Defenders of the Constitution".

More in tune with the Duma on foreign policy, Yeltsin also sent a strong signal on Friday to the West -- and to a domestic audience -- that Russia wanted NATO to abandon any idea of integrating former Soviet republics into the Western alliance.
Forecasting his talks with Clinton "will be the hardest in all the history of Russian-American relations", Yeltsin said Moscow would make no concession that would weaken its defences.

But he added: "In a recent telephone conversation Clinton made clear the United States is interested in compromise, and so am I. We are for a compromise which would not abuse the security of the Russian Federation."
